prompt: A dock supervisor points at drums of paint thinner and asks which hazard class covers that solvent before it goes on your trailer. Which class should you expect on those solvent drums?

options.text: Flammable liquids, the hazard class for that solvent
Explosives, the class used when a load can detonate
Gases, the class used for cylinders under pressure
Corrosives, the class used for acid that eats metal

explanation: Paint thinner and similar solvents are Class 3 flammable liquids. Class 1 is explosives, Class 2 is gases, and Class 8 is corrosives, so the diamond on those drums follows the liquid, not a neighboring class.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Class 3 flammable liquids with Class 1 explosives. Detonation is the explosives class, not the class for solvent.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a flammable liquid with Class 2 gases. A drum of solvent is not a compressed-gas cylinder.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Class 3 with Class 8 corrosives. Acid that eats metal is a different class from paint thinner.

prompt: During a gate inspection an officer asks what job the large diamond on your trailer is meant to do for people who never open the paperwork. What is that diamond mainly for?

options.text: Replace the paperwork on a short local delivery
Communicate the hazard of the materials on the vehicle
Name the offeror and the receiver on the trailer doors
Show the packing group of every package in the van

explanation: A placard tells responders and the public the hazard of what is on the vehicle. It does not replace shipping papers, name the parties, or list a packing group for each package.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the diamond with a paperwork waiver. Papers still travel with the shipment; the diamond does not stand in for them.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a placard with the parties named on the papers. The diamond shows the hazard, not who shipped or who receives.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the vehicle diamond with a packing-group entry. Packing group is written on the papers, not as the placard's job.

prompt: Before the night departure you search your cab for the hazardous materials documents and wonder where they must sit once you are behind the wheel. Where do those documents belong?

options.text: Locked in a toolbox on the trailer you cannot open quickly
Left on the dispatch desk so the pages stay clean
Within immediate reach while you are at the controls
Sent ahead so only the receiver holds a copy en route

explanation: While you are at the controls, hazardous materials shipping papers must be within immediate reach so you or a responder can get them without a search. A locked trailer box, the office, or a copy mailed ahead fails that duty.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses secure storage with ready access. A toolbox you cannot open from the seat hides the papers from an inspector or a responder.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a clean file at the terminal with papers that must travel. The documents have to be in the cab while you drive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses delivery copies with the set that rides with the load. The driver needs the papers during the trip, not only the receiver.

prompt: Beside the highway a trooper compares the code printed on your papers with the code on the vehicle and asks what kind of number that code is. What is that identification number?

options.text: The single class digit shown in a placard corner
The guidebook page a responder would open first
A packing group written out as a long numeric code
A four-digit UN or NA identification number

explanation: The identification number on the papers and on the vehicle is a four-digit UN or NA number for that material. It is not the class digit, a guidebook page, or a packing-group mark.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the four-digit identification number with the hazard class digit in the placard corner. Those are different marks.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the identification number with a page in the emergency guidebook. The number on the papers is the UN or NA code.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the identification number with a packing group. Packing groups are roman numerals, not the four-digit material code.

prompt: Cases of blasting caps ride on your trailer and the papers mark them Division 1.1. A helper asks what that division means if one case lets go. What hazard does Division 1.1 describe?

options.text: A mass explosion hazard if the load lets go
Mainly a projection hazard, as in Division 1.2
Mainly a fire hazard, as in Division 1.3
Only a minor blast, as in Division 1.4 articles

explanation: Division 1.1 explosives present a mass explosion hazard: if one item initiates, the load can explode together. Division 1.2 is mainly projection, 1.3 is mainly fire, and 1.4 is a minor blast hazard.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Division 1.1 with Division 1.2. Projection is the 1.2 hazard; 1.1 is a mass explosion.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Division 1.1 with Division 1.3. A fire-dominant explosive hazard is 1.3, not the mass-explosion division.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Division 1.1 with Division 1.4. A minor blast is the lower division; 1.1 is the mass-explosion hazard.

prompt: Standing beside a gasoline cargo tank your trainer taps the diamond and asks which color drivers should expect on a flammable-liquid placard. Which color is that Class 3 diamond?

options.text: Orange, the field used for an explosive placard
Red, the color used for flammable liquids
Blue, the field used when a solid is dangerous if wet
Green, the field used for a non-flammable gas

explanation: A Class 3 flammable-liquid placard is red, which is the color you should see on that gasoline tank. Orange is explosives, blue is dangerous when wet, and green is non-flammable gas.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the red Class 3 placard with the orange field used for explosives. Gasoline is not an explosive placard.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Class 3 red with the blue dangerous-when-wet placard. Wet-reactive solids are not flammable liquids.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Class 3 red with the green non-flammable-gas placard. A gasoline tank is not a Division 2.2 load.

prompt: Once the dock spill is contained a firefighter opens the orange guidebook and asks what that book is supposed to give you in the first minutes. What is the guidebook for?

options.text: The weight cutoffs that decide when a diamond is required
Which classes must stay apart while you load the trailer
Initial isolation, evacuation, and fire or spill steps
A stand-in for the shipping papers on a short haul

explanation: The Emergency Response Guidebook gives first actions: isolation, evacuation, and how to handle a fire or a spill. Placard cutoffs, load separation, and the shipping papers live in other rules and documents.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the guidebook with the placarding tables. Weight cutoffs decide diamonds; the guidebook is for the first emergency steps.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the guidebook with segregation rules used at loading. The orange book is initial response, not a loading chart.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the guidebook with the shipping papers. You still carry the papers; the book does not replace them.

prompt: Separate non-bulk categories from Table 2 share space on one trailer and both would need placards. When may a single DANGEROUS diamond stand in for those separate class diamonds?

options.text: When any Table 1 material, such as an explosive, is aboard
When one bulk package of a single class is the only freight
When one Table 2 category is aboard and already has its own diamond
When non-bulk packages of two or more categories require placards

explanation: A DANGEROUS placard may be used for non-bulk packages of two or more Table 2 categories that require placarding, when the rules allow that option. It does not cover a Table 1 material, a single bulk package, or one category that already takes its own placard.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the DANGEROUS option with Table 1. Explosives and other Table 1 materials keep their own placards at any amount.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses mixed non-bulk Table 2 freight with one bulk package. A single bulk package is not the DANGEROUS substitution case.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a mixed load with one Table 2 category. One category that needs a placard uses that class diamond, not DANGEROUS.

prompt: A warehouse clerk holds a drum whose papers say Class 8 and asks what kind of material that class covers before you sign for the load. What are Class 8 materials?

options.text: Corrosives that can burn skin or eat through metal
Explosives that can detonate across the whole load
Flammable gases that ignite when a cylinder leaks
Miscellaneous materials that fall only under Class 9

explanation: Class 8 is corrosives: materials that can burn living tissue or eat through metal. Explosives are Class 1, flammable gases are Division 2.1, and miscellaneous hazardous materials are Class 9.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Class 8 corrosives with Class 1 explosives. Detonation is not what the corrosive class describes.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Class 8 with Division 2.1 flammable gas. A leaking cylinder of gas is not the corrosive class.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Class 8 with Class 9. Miscellaneous hazardous materials are their own class, not corrosives.

prompt: While building the basic description the clerk asks which entries have to appear together so responders can identify the product fast. What does that basic description include?

options.text: A nickname, the offeror's street, and a guidebook page
ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, and packing group
A trade name, a delivery window, and a piece count
Quantity, trailer number, receiver city, and a time slot

explanation: The basic description is the identification number, the proper shipping name, the hazard class or division, and the packing group when one is assigned. Nicknames, addresses, piece counts, and appointment details are not that sequence.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the basic description with extra entries. A nickname, a street, and a guidebook page are not the four-part description.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the proper shipping name with a trade name, and swaps in a delivery window and a piece count that sit outside the basic description.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the basic description with trip details. Quantity can be added elsewhere; trailer number, city, and a time slot are not the description.

prompt: Next to the product name the solvent paperwork shows Packing Group I, and a new hire thinks that mark means the product is mild. What does Packing Group I indicate?

options.text: The least danger, so ordinary freight handling is enough
Medium danger, the middle step of the three groups
Great danger, the highest of the three packing groups
An explosive risk that replaces the hazard class

explanation: Packing Group I means great danger, the highest of the three groups. Packing Group II is medium danger and Packing Group III is minor danger. The group does not turn the product into an explosive.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Packing Group I with Packing Group III. The least danger is Group III; Group I is great danger.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Packing Group I with Packing Group II. Medium danger is the middle group, not the highest.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a packing group with Class 1. Great danger in Group I does not replace the hazard class with an explosive class.

prompt: A pallet of sulfur matches is offered for your trailer and the shipper calls them a flammable solid. Which material class includes flammable solids such as those matches?

options.text: Class 2, home of Division 2.1 flammable gases
Class 3, home of flammable liquids such as solvent
Class 5, home of oxidizers and organic peroxides
Class 4, including Division 4.1 flammable solids

explanation: Flammable solids belong in Class 4, and Division 4.1 is the flammable-solid division that covers a product like sulfur matches. Flammable gases are Class 2, flammable liquids are Class 3, and oxidizers are Class 5.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Division 4.1 flammable solids with Division 2.1 flammable gases. Matches are not a gas class.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Class 4 solids with Class 3 flammable liquids. A solvent is a liquid class; the matches are solids.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses flammable solids with Class 5 oxidizers and organic peroxides. Those feed a fire; they are not Division 4.1.

prompt: Printed on a fiberboard box of solvent you see a small diamond set square on a point, and a helper thinks it is the same mark you hang on the trailer. What does that package diamond indicate?

options.text: A hazard label warning what is inside that package
The vehicle placard you must also hang on the trailer
A handling mark that shows which side of the box faces up
A guidebook page number printed for responders

explanation: The small square-on-point mark on a non-bulk package is a hazard label for what is inside. The larger placard goes on the vehicle. Up-arrows are orientation marks, and guidebook pages are not printed as that diamond.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a package label with a vehicle placard. The diamond on the box warns about that package; the placard is the larger vehicle mark.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the hazard label with orientation arrows. Which side faces up is a handling mark, not the class diamond.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the package label with a guidebook page. The diamond identifies the hazard class, not a page number.

prompt: Listed beside a gas cylinder the division reads 2.3, and your partner guesses it is just another flammable liquid. What does Division 2.3 refer to on those papers?

options.text: Flammable gas, which is Division 2.1 instead
Poison gas, a toxic gas under Division 2.3
Non-flammable gas, which is Division 2.2 instead
A poisonous liquid, which is Division 6.1 instead

explanation: Division 2.3 is poison gas, also called toxic gas. Division 2.1 is flammable gas, Division 2.2 is non-flammable gas, and a poisonous liquid is Division 6.1, not a gas division.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Division 2.3 poison gas with Division 2.1 flammable gas. A gas that burns is 2.1, not the toxic-gas division.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Division 2.3 with Division 2.2. Non-flammable gas is 2.2; 2.3 is the poison-gas division.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a toxic gas with Division 6.1 poisonous liquids or solids. Division 2.3 is the gas, not a liquid poison class.

prompt: As the freight is offered for transport the clerk asks who must get the classification and the description right before the carrier is allowed to accept it. Who holds that duty?

options.text: The receiver, who is expected to classify the freight on arrival
The driver alone, leaving the offeror with no duty to describe it
The shipper, while the carrier still checks before accepting
The loader, whose handling work replaces a written description

explanation: The shipper must classify and describe the hazardous material before offering it. The carrier still has to check the papers, marks, and placards and may refuse a shipment that does not comply.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the shipper's offer duty with the receiver. Classification and the description are owed before the trip, not after arrival.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the shipper's duty with the driver's. The carrier checks and complies, but that does not erase the shipper's duty to describe the load.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a written description with physical handling. Moving the freight does not replace classification and the shipping description.

prompt: Pointing at dynamite and then at gasoline a trainee swaps the class numbers and asks you to sort the pair. Which pairing matches those two products?

options.text: Class 1 is flammable liquids and Class 3 is the explosives group
Class 1 is poison gas and Class 3 is a corrosive that eats metal
Class 1 is radioactive material and Class 3 is an oxidizer solid
Class 1 is explosives and Class 3 is flammable liquids

explanation: Dynamite is Class 1, explosives. Gasoline is Class 3, flammable liquids. Swapping those numbers puts the explosive class on the fuel and the liquid class on the dynamite.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps Class 1 and Class 3. Explosives are Class 1 and flammable liquids are Class 3, not the other way around.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns poison gas and a corrosive to this pair. Those are Division 2.3 and Class 8, not dynamite and gasoline.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns radioactive material and an oxidizer. Those are Class 7 and Class 5, not the explosive and the flammable liquid.

prompt: Marked flammable on the manifest those propane cylinders make a coworker insist they belong with gasoline. Which class is correct for that flammable gas?

options.text: Class 2, because that flammable gas is not a Class 3 liquid
Class 3, because any product that can burn is treated as a flammable liquid
Class 4, because a gas that ignites is grouped with flammable solids
Class 8, because pressure in the cylinder is treated as a corrosive hazard

explanation: Propane is a flammable gas, so it is Class 2, not Class 3. A product that burns is not automatically a flammable liquid; the class follows the form on the papers, and a gas stays with the gases.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a flammable gas with Class 3 flammable liquids. Gasoline is the liquid class; propane cylinders are gases.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Class 2 gas with Class 4 flammable solids. Ignition does not move a cylinder into the solids class.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses cylinder pressure with Class 8 corrosives. Pressure does not make a flammable gas into a corrosive.

prompt: Leaking acid from wet batteries makes the loader reach for a poison diamond because the liquid looks harmful. Unless the papers say otherwise, which class fits that acid?

options.text: Class 6 poison, because any harmful liquid is grouped with toxic substances
Class 8 corrosive, not a Class 6 poison unless the papers differ
Class 3, because battery acid is shipped like a flammable solvent
Class 9, because a wet battery counts as ordinary miscellaneous freight

explanation: A battery wet with acid is a Class 8 corrosive unless the papers say otherwise. Class 6 is poisons. Looking harmful is not a reason to hang a poison diamond on an acid battery.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a corrosive acid with Class 6 poison. Toxicity and corrosion are different classes; this acid battery is the corrosive.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses battery acid with Class 3 flammable liquids. A solvent diamond does not describe a wet acid battery.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Class 8 with Class 9 miscellaneous materials, and treats a regulated battery as ordinary freight.

prompt: Offered as one small radioactive package the material is Class 7, and the loader says the size lets you skip any diamond. What should you do about placarding that shipment?

options.text: Skip the diamond because the package is small and looks minor on the dock
Call it Class 9 and hang a miscellaneous diamond instead of following Class 7
Follow the shipping papers and the placard table, not the package size
Treat the package as a Class 8 corrosive and placard it as acid

explanation: Class 7 is radioactive. A small package is not a reason to skip placarding. Follow the shipping papers and the placard table, including Table 1 at any amount when that material is one the table covers.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats package size as an exemption. Small does not make a Class 7 placard optional; the papers and the table decide.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Class 7 radioactive material with Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous materials. The class on the papers stays Class 7.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses radioactive material with a Class 8 corrosive. An acid placard does not describe a Class 7 package.

prompt: Comparing a Table 1 line with Table 2 freight on the same dispatch sheet, you have to decide when each kind of material forces a diamond. When does each table require placarding?

options.text: Table 1 only after 1,001 pounds, and Table 2 for any amount riding on the truck
Both tables only after the receiver asks for diamonds at the delivery dock
Neither table, because two different lines on one sheet cancel placarding
Table 1 materials at any amount, and Table 2 at 1,001 pounds or more

explanation: Table 1 materials are placarded at any amount. Table 2 materials are placarded at 1,001 pounds or more. Swapping those cutoffs, waiting for the receiver, or cancelling both lines leaves the vehicle wrong.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the two tables. Table 1 is any amount; the 1,001-pound line is the Table 2 threshold, not the Table 1 rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a regulatory placard with a customer request. The tables decide, not a request at the delivery dock.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a mixed sheet as a cancellation. Each table still applies to its own materials.

prompt: Mixed Table 2 freight may take a substitute diamond when the rules allow it, and a Table 1 explosive is sitting in another bay. Which diamond may you use for that mixed Table 2 freight?

options.text: The DANGEROUS placard for mixed Table 2 freight when the rules allow it
A DANGEROUS diamond in place of the Table 1 explosive placard that bay still requires
No diamond at all, because two Table 2 classes cancel each other on one trailer
A Class 9 diamond, because mixed Table 2 freight counts as miscellaneous material

explanation: When the rules allow it, mixed Table 2 freight may display the DANGEROUS placard instead of a separate placard for each category. Do not use DANGEROUS in place of a Table 1 placard, which that explosive still needs at any amount.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses DANGEROUS to cover a Table 1 explosive. Table 1 materials keep their own placards; DANGEROUS is not a substitute for them.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats two Table 2 classes as a reason to drop placards. Mixing categories does not cancel a placard the rules require.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses mixed Table 2 freight with Class 9 miscellaneous material. A Class 9 diamond does not replace the DANGEROUS option.

prompt: Required diamonds are due on this trailer and the yard boss hangs one only on the rear doors, claiming traffic behind you is all that matters. Where must those diamonds be displayed?

options.text: On the rear doors alone, where following traffic can read a single diamond
On all four sides: front, rear, and both sides of the vehicle
On the cab door beside the paperwork, and nowhere on the cargo body
On the front bumper so oncoming traffic sees the hazard before passing

explanation: When placards are required they go on all four sides of the vehicle: front, rear, and both sides. One diamond on the rear, a cab-door mark, or a bumper-only mark leaves the other sides bare.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the rear doors. Following traffic is one view; a required placard still has to appear on all four sides.
distractorExplanations.c: Puts the mark by the paperwork in the cab. The placard belongs on the vehicle sides, not only next to the papers.
distractorExplanations.d: Covers oncoming traffic and skips the other three sides. The front alone does not finish a required placard display.

prompt: Displayed on an orange panel the tank shows an identification number, and a white panel on the diamond could show one too. You do not trust your memory. Which number do you display?

options.text: A code you remember from a similar product you hauled on an earlier trip
The class digit in the placard corner, used as if it were the identification code
The identification number on the panel that matches the shipping papers
The trailer unit number painted along the side of the tank

explanation: The identification number on an orange panel, or on a white panel on the placard, must match the shipping papers. Do not pick a code from memory, use the class digit, or paint the trailer unit number in that spot.

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes memory of an earlier load for the papers. A similar product can carry a different identification number.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the identification number with the class digit in the placard corner. The panel has to show the number from the papers.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the material identification number with the trailer unit number. The fleet number does not identify the hazardous material.

prompt: After the walkaround you tuck the shipping packet beneath a pillow in the sleeper so the cab looks tidy for the trip. Where must that packet ride while you drive?

options.text: Under the sleeper pillow, as long as you can find the packet at the next fuel stop
In a locked outside box where wind cannot pull the pages loose
Back in the terminal file, with a note that the load was already checked
Within the driver's reach while driving, tabbed or on top of the other papers

explanation: Hazardous materials papers must be within the driver's reach and tabbed or on top so the hazardous entries are obvious. The sleeper berth, a locked outside box, and a file left at the terminal all fail that rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the sleeper as good enough storage. A pillow in the berth is not within reach at the controls, and the packet is not tabbed or on top.
distractorExplanations.b: Hides the packet where you cannot reach it while belted. Wind protection does not satisfy the reach rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves the packet at the terminal. The papers have to ride where you can produce them during the trip.

prompt: Written by the buyer a nickname sits where the regulated product name should be, and the class and code are missing. Which entries do the papers have to show?

options.text: The proper shipping name, the hazard class, and the identification number
The buyer's nickname, a color name, and the purchase order for the account
The brand painted on the drum, with no class and no identification number beside it
The receiver's pet name for the product and the delivery appointment

explanation: The papers must use the proper shipping name, the hazard class, and the identification number. A customer nickname, a brand painted on the drum, or a pet name is not the proper shipping name.

distractorExplanations.b: Accepts a nickname plus a color and a purchase order. None of those is the proper shipping name, the class, or the identification number.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops at a brand on the drum and drops the class and the identification number the description requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a pet name and an appointment for the regulated description. The receiver's wording is not the proper shipping name.

prompt: Shown as Class 9 the regulated waste makes a coworker say the freight is ordinary and needs no hazard treatment at all. What does Class 9 actually mean?

options.text: Explosives that did not fit a lower division inside Class 1
Miscellaneous hazardous materials, not non-hazardous freight
Mild flammable liquids that are too weak for a Class 3 diamond on the trailer
Non-hazardous freight that needs no description and no diamond anywhere

explanation: Class 9 is miscellaneous hazardous materials. It is still a hazardous class. Calling the waste non-hazardous, or shoving it into explosives or flammable liquids, misreads the papers.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Class 9 with Class 1 explosives. A leftover explosive division is not what miscellaneous hazardous materials means.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Class 9 with a weak Class 3 liquid. Flammable liquids stay in Class 3; Class 9 is the miscellaneous hazardous class.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads Class 9 as non-hazardous. Miscellaneous means a hazardous material that does not fall in Classes 1 through 8, not ordinary freight.

prompt: Treated like paint thinner an oxidizer drum is loaded as if it were a flammable liquid because both can worsen a fire. Which class covers oxidizers and organic peroxides?

options.text: Class 3, because a product that worsens a fire is a flammable liquid
Class 2, because oxidizers are hauled as compressed gas cylinders
Class 5, oxidizers and organic peroxides that feed a fire
Class 8, because an oxidizer eats metal the way battery acid does

explanation: Class 5 is oxidizers and organic peroxides. An oxidizer feeds a fire by supplying oxygen; it is not a Class 3 flammable liquid. Do not hang the red liquid diamond just because fire is part of the hazard.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an oxidizer with Class 3 flammable liquids. Worsening a fire is not the same as being the fuel liquid.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Class 5 oxidizers with Class 2 gases. An oxidizer drum is not automatically a compressed-gas cylinder.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an oxidizer with a Class 8 corrosive. Feeding a fire is not the same hazard as acid that eats metal.

prompt: Faded by sun the rear diamond has lost its symbol and its words, and dispatch says a worn diamond still counts for the trip. What must you do before you roll?

options.text: Leave the worn diamond, because a faded mark still counts as a displayed placard
Flip the diamond so the blank back faces traffic and hides the fade
Tape over the fade and handwrite a class digit on the tape
Replace the faded placard before you roll, because you cannot read it

explanation: A placard you cannot read because it is faded is not in compliance. Replace it before you roll. A worn diamond, a flipped blank side, or handwriting on tape does not restore a readable placard.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a faded placard as still displayed. If the symbol and words are gone, the placard is not readable and does not count.
distractorExplanations.b: Hides the placard instead of replacing it. A blank back toward traffic is not a readable hazard display.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes tape and handwriting for a proper placard. A class digit on tape is not a maintained placard.

prompt: Signed by the shipper the certification is on the papers, yet the diamonds do not match the papers or the drums you can see on the trailer. What do you do with that load?

options.text: Refuse the load until the papers, the placards, and the freight you see all match
Accept it, because the shipper's signature ends any duty to compare what you see
Haul it and correct the diamonds after you arrive at the receiver's dock
Hang any spare diamond from the cab so the trailer looks marked for the scale house

explanation: The shipper certifies the papers, but you still refuse a load when the papers, the placards, and the freight you see do not match. A signature does not make a mismatch legal to haul.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the shipper's certification as the end of your check. You still compare papers, placards, and what is actually on the trailer.
distractorExplanations.c: Delays the fix until delivery. A mismatch is a reason to refuse before you roll, not a problem to patch at the receiver.
distractorExplanations.d: Hangs a spare diamond so the trailer looks marked. A random placard that does not match the papers or the drums is still wrong.

prompt: Looking empty the returned drums still hold a residue film, and the shipper tells you to pull the diamonds because nothing will pour out. What is the right call on those drums?

options.text: Pull every diamond, because a drum that looks empty is no longer a regulated hazardous material
Keep diamonds only when a full drum of the same product is loaded beside the residue
Haul the drums as ordinary trash with no hazard entry left on the papers
Residue can stay hazardous, so keep the placards the rules still require on the drums

explanation: Empty packages that still hold residue can remain hazardous. Looking empty, or hearing that nothing will pour out, is not a reason to drop placards the rules still require.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a dry-looking drum as unregulated. Residue can keep the hazard, so pulling every placard because it looks empty is the miss.
distractorExplanations.b: Ties the placard to a full drum sitting beside the residue. The residue itself can still require the placards the rules call for.
distractorExplanations.c: Reclassifies residue as ordinary trash and drops the hazard entry. Appearance does not cancel a description or a placard the rules still require.

prompt: A dock supervisor tells you to stack a pallet of corrosives directly against a pallet of cyanides because both fit the last row of the trailer. How should those incompatible hazardous materials be loaded?

options.text: Segregated according to the segregation tables
Loaded together when every package still looks undamaged
Stacked in the sequence already printed on the shipping papers
Placed by weight, with the heavier class sitting on the deck

explanation: Corrosives braced against cyanides are incompatible hazardous materials, so the segregation table decides the load. A last row that happens to fit both pallets does not authorize that pair to ride in contact.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses intact packaging with compatibility. An undamaged drum can still be forbidden beside another class, and the segregation table makes that call.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes shipping-paper order with segregation. The papers list what you carry; they do not authorize two incompatible classes to touch.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats deck position and weight as a substitute for class separation. Heavier-on-the-floor is a securement habit, not a segregation rule.

prompt: At a chemical warehouse the forklift operator wants to drop five liquid drums into a tight cluster and leave them unbraced so the trailer can leave before the lunch break. What must you do with those hazmat packages before you roll?

options.text: Drag the drums by their chimes so the cluster can be built faster
Protect the packages from damage and secure them against movement
Lay the liquid drums on their sides so the stack height drops
Leave the cluster loose at the dock and strap it after you are already rolling

explanation: Those liquid drums have to be protected from damage and secured against movement before the trailer rolls. A tight cluster with no bracing can shift, stress closures, and leak once the vehicle is moving.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses speed of handling with package care. Hooks and chime-dragging can puncture or dent hazmat drums, which loading rules do not allow.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes a lower stack with safe orientation. Laying liquid drums on their sides fights the upright marks and can leak at the closures.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats securement as something you finish after departure. Packages must be blocked and braced before the vehicle moves, not once the load has already shifted.

prompt: A winter dispatcher offers to leave the cargo heater running in a van that will carry flammable liquid drums overnight so the product does not thicken. Why are burning heaters restricted around that kind of hazmat?

options.text: Heaters pull reserve air the trailer brakes need to stay charged
A heated van must display an extra placard that a cold van does not
Heat and ignition sources can trigger a fire or an explosion
Heat raises the packing group of every product loaded in the van

explanation: A burning cargo heater is an ignition source beside flammable liquid. The restriction exists because heat and ignition can trigger a fire or an explosion, not because the product might thicken overnight.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses heater limits with the air-brake system. The ban is about ignition around flammables and explosives, not about air supply for the brakes.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a placard for a heated cargo space. No such placard exists; heaters are restricted because they can ignite flammable cargo.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes temperature with classification. Packing group is assigned to the material and does not climb because a heater is running.

prompt: A trainer points at a cargo tank of gasoline and a carton of small paint cans and asks why one is treated as bulk and the other as non-bulk under the hazmat rules. What primarily separates those two package types?

options.text: Whether a placard has already been stuck on the package
The hazard class and packing group printed on the label
Whether the shipper listed an emergency response contact
Capacity thresholds defined in the HMR

explanation: Bulk and non-bulk are separated by capacity thresholds defined in the Hazardous Materials Regulations. The gasoline tank and the small paint cans are different package types because of capacity, not because of the class name on the label.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses placarding with the bulk definition. A placard follows from what you ship; bulk versus non-bulk is a capacity threshold in the rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes hazard classification with package size. Class and packing group describe the danger; bulk status depends on capacity thresholds.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the emergency contact as the bulk test. That contact is a shipping-paper item for hazmat either way; capacity is what splits bulk from non-bulk.

prompt: You are about to load Division 1.1 explosives at a magazine, and the yard boss says the van is fine because it hauled produce yesterday. What should you confirm about that vehicle before the explosives go aboard?

options.text: The vehicle is appropriate and free of ignition hazards
The cargo floor is bare steel so static can drain away
The cargo heater is lit so the detonators stay dry
Blasting caps may ride loose beside the Division 1.1 cases

explanation: Before Class 1 explosives are loaded, the vehicle has to be appropriate and free of ignition hazards. Yesterday's produce haul does not make a van acceptable if a heater, spark, or other ignition source is still in play.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses static control with a bare metal deck. Explosives want a tight floor that will not spark, not exposed steel left uncovered.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a cargo heater as protection for detonators. A heater is an ignition source and is restricted around explosives, so it stays off.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes detonators with Division 1.1 in one loose pile. Those items do not ride together unless the segregation rules and authorized packagings allow it.

prompt: Before you roll a pallet of flammable paint into an older trailer, you notice popped screws and a film of oil across the deck. What condition should that hazmat cargo floor meet?

options.text: Oiled so the heavy drums slide into the nose without a fight
Clean and free of nails or screws that could puncture packages
Covered with loose straw so every carton has a soft bed
Left with proud nails so the straps have something to hook

explanation: A hazmat cargo floor should be clean and free of nails or screws that could puncture packages. Oil and popped screws on this older deck can shift the paint or pierce a container before you ever leave the yard.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an easy slide with a safe deck. Oil lets drums move and can contaminate the freight; the floor needs to be clean, not slick.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes cushioning with the floor rule. Loose straw adds fuel and debris; the requirement is a clean deck without projections, plus real securement.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats protruding nails as tie points. Those points puncture packages, so they are removed or made flush rather than used as hooks.

prompt: A shipper clerk wants an acid drum and a cyanide drum braced in the same corner because the segregation chart is back in the office. Why must those two materials stay apart if a package fails?

options.text: They would combine into ordinary table salt and become harmless
Their placards would cancel and make the pair legal in one corner
Together they can release toxic hydrogen cyanide gas
The mixture would become Class 9 and count as a safe load

explanation: Acids and cyanides are kept apart because a leak from both can release toxic hydrogen cyanide gas. A missing chart in the office does not make that corner a safe place to brace the two drums together.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses this pair with a harmless neutralization. Acid plus cyanide in a cargo leak is not a path to table salt; it can liberate a toxic gas.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes placard display with chemistry. Placards do not cancel each other, and two labels on one trailer do not make an incompatible pair legal.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the reaction product as a mild Class 9. The hazard of that mix is toxic gas, not a downgrade to a miscellaneous safe load.

prompt: After a gasoline cargo tank finishes loading, the rack attendant walks off and leaves the manhole cover resting on the rim. What should the manhole covers and valves be before you move that tank?

options.text: Left cracked open so vapor pressure can bleed off on the road
Closed after the product is pumped off at the receiver
Closed by the loader, so the driver does not need to look
Closed and secured per procedures, then checked for leaks

explanation: Before a loaded gasoline cargo tank moves, manhole covers and valves are closed and secured per procedures, then checked for leaks. A cover resting on the rim is an open path for product to leave the tank in transit.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an open manhole with normal venting. Pressure relief is built into the tank; covers and valves stay closed while you are on the road.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes unloading with the pre-trip close. Covers and valves are secured before the loaded tank moves, not for the first time after delivery.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the loader's walk-away as the driver's check. You still verify that manholes and valves are closed and not leaking before you roll.

prompt: A grocery backhaul includes sealed cartons marked toxic that a lumper wants stacked on boxed produce because the trailer is short on floor space. Where should those toxic packages ride?

options.text: Away from foodstuffs and per the separation rules
On the produce, provided every toxic carton is still sealed
In the cab, where you would notice a leak right away
Against the rear doors, so any fumes blow out while driving

explanation: Cartons marked toxic are loaded away from foodstuffs and under the separation rules. A short floor and intact seals do not let those cartons sit on boxed produce in the same unseparated space.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a sealed package with permission to touch food. Toxic materials and foodstuffs still follow the separation rules even when every carton looks intact.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes watchfulness with the cargo location. Toxic packages do not ride in the driver's compartment so a leak would be easier to smell.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the rear doors as a vent for a leaking poison. A package placed to vent is a package you expect to leak, and a leaking toxic package is not loaded.

prompt: While you are building a mixed hazmat load, a corrosive jug in the staging lane is wet at the cap and dripping onto the dock plate. What should happen to that leaking package?

options.text: Wipe the cap, tape it, and set the jug on the truck
Not loaded; protect people and notify the appropriate parties
Stand it upright, pack absorbent at the base, and then load it
Load it now and tell the shipper after you arrive

explanation: A corrosive jug already dripping on the dock plate is not loaded. Protect people around the leak and notify the appropriate parties at the dock, before that package ever goes on the truck.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a field patch with an acceptable package. Wiping and taping a dripping jug does not make a leaking hazmat package legal to transport.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes spill cleanup with acceptance. Absorbent can help contain a drip on the dock, but it does not turn a leaking jug into freight you may load.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the report until delivery. The leaking package stays off the vehicle, and the notice happens before any transport, not at the receiver.

prompt: You are hauling a placarded flammable-liquid load when the highway ramp ends at a railroad grade crossing that is not one of the exempt crossings. What must you do at that crossing?

options.text: Slow down, look both ways, and cross without making a stop
Stop on the nearest rail, then cross in the highest gear
Stop, with the listed exceptions, listen, and go only when safe
Stop short of the tracks, then shift gears while you are crossing

explanation: At a required railroad crossing, a placarded vehicle stops 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail, listens, and proceeds only when safe, using a gear that does not have to be shifted on the tracks. Listed exceptions exist, so this is not a stop at every rail you see.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a cautious roll with the required stop. Looking both ways without stopping does not meet the rule for a placarded vehicle at a crossing that is not exempt.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes the stop location with a gear choice. You do not stop on the rail, and you do not cross in a gear you will have to change on the tracks.
distractorExplanations.d: Gets the idea of stopping, then adds a prohibited shift. Select a gear that lets you clear the crossing without shifting while you are on the rails.

prompt: Two incompatible compressed gas cylinders are lying loose against each other behind the last pallet, and the loader says the caps make that acceptable. Why is that loose pairing unsafe?

options.text: A loose cylinder matters when the gas inside is flammable
Valve caps by themselves make a loose cylinder acceptable in a van
Gas segregation applies to cargo tanks but not to cylinders in a van
Damaged valves or releases can cause fire, asphyxiation, or toxic exposure

explanation: Loose incompatible cylinders can damage valves and release gas. That release can cause fire, asphyxiation, or toxic exposure, so caps alone do not make the pairing safe behind the last pallet.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the hazard with flammable gas alone. A nonflammable release can still asphyxiate, and oxidizers or toxics create other harm; every cylinder is secured.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes a valve cap with full securement. Caps protect valves, but the cylinders still have to be secured and segregated rather than left loose.
distractorExplanations.c: Limits the segregation table to cargo tanks. The table applies to packages on the transport vehicle, including cylinders loaded in a van.

prompt: A row of liquid cartons shows double arrows pointing up, and a helper wants to lay them flat so one more layer fits under the roof bow. What do those orientation arrows require of you?

options.text: Keep the package upright as marked
Stack those cartons no more than two layers high
Point the marked end toward the nose of the trailer
Slow the forklift, because the mark means the goods are fragile

explanation: Orientation arrows mean keep the package upright as marked. Laying those liquid cartons flat to gain a layer under the roof bow can stress closures and leak, even if the extra layer would fit.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses orientation arrows with a stack-height mark. A separate stacking mark limits layers; these arrows show which way is up.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes an up-arrow with a front-of-trailer direction. The arrows show vertical orientation so closures stay up, not which end faces the nose.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the arrows as a fragile-handling mark. Fragility uses a different mark; these arrows require the carton to travel upright as marked.

prompt: Your reefer is set for produce, and the shipper adds poison packages to the same trailer because the temperature looks low enough to keep everything fresh. What must you do when hazmat and food share a trip?

options.text: Set the poison packages directly on top of the produce
Comply with contamination prevention and separation rules; some combinations are forbidden
Skip the food rules because this trailer is running as a refrigerator
Use spare produce as absorbent if a poison package starts to leak

explanation: When hazmat and food share a trip, you comply with contamination prevention and separation rules, and some combinations are forbidden. A cold reefer setpoint does not make poison packages acceptable beside produce.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a space-saving stack with the food rule. Putting poison directly on produce is the contamination the separation rules are written to prevent.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes refrigeration with a waiver. A cold trailer does not cancel contamination prevention or the combinations the rules forbid.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats food as spill control. Produce is cargo to protect, not an absorbent for a poison leak.

prompt: A tight looking stack of hazmat drums has no blocking, and the yard driver says friction alone will hold it on a straight highway run. Why does securement still matter if that stack shifts?

options.text: Shifting weight changes which placards the trailer must display
The shipping papers become void until someone rebuilds the stack
Movement can damage packages, open closures, and cause spills
Sliding drums raise the packing group of the materials on board

explanation: Securement matters because movement can damage packages, open closures, and cause spills. Friction on a straight highway is not blocking, and a shift can also let released materials meet a class they should not touch.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses load position with placarding. Placards follow what is aboard, not where a drum slides; the harm from movement is damaged packages and leaks.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes a shifted stack with voided papers. The papers stay in effect; the danger is open closures and a release, not a canceled bill.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a slide as reclassification. Packing group is fixed by the material; shifting cargo causes damage and spills, not a higher packing group.

prompt: The leftover floor will accept either a flammable pallet or an oxidizer pallet, and the loader says to take whichever cube happens to fit. What should decide whether those groups share this vehicle?

options.text: Segregate by the table, not by what fits
Load whichever pallet happens to fill the leftover floor space
Put the milder group in the nose and call that position separation
Accept both pallets if every label on them is still readable

explanation: You do not load hazmat by whichever pallet cubes into the leftover floor. Flammables and oxidizers share a vehicle only if the segregation table allows that pair, not because both happen to fit.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses leftover floor space with compatibility. Which pallet cubes out the trailer is not the segregation decision; the table is.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes nose position with separation. Putting a milder group in front does not replace the segregation table for that pair.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a readable label as permission to mix classes. Labels identify the hazard; they do not let a forbidden pair share the vehicle.

prompt: A produce shipper asks you to drop poison cases into the same undivided trailer and throw a tarp over the food, claiming that cover is enough separation. Which decision matches the food-and-poison rule?

options.text: Haul both and treat a tarp over the food as full separation
Put the poison in the nose and the food against the rear doors
Accept the mix if the reefer stays cold for the whole trip
Keep food and poison out of one unseparated space

explanation: A food load and a poison do not share an unseparated space. Follow the segregation and separation rules, and do not guess that a tarp thrown over the produce is enough separation for those poison cases.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a tarp with required separation. A cover over the food does not create the separation the rules demand between poison and a food load.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes door position with separation. Nose versus rear doors inside one undivided trailer is still one unseparated space for food and poison.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a cold setpoint as a waiver. Temperature does not let poison cases share an unseparated trailer with food.

prompt: After the forklift squares a wall of solvent drums, the loader says the stack looks tight enough and blocking would only waste time before the gate. Is that wall actually secured for the road?

options.text: Yes. A squared wall holds itself, so blocking and bracing are optional
No. A tight look with no blocking is not secured
Yes. Plastic drums cannot shift once they are squared in a van
Strap the top row and leave the floor layer free to settle on its own

explanation: Secure packages against movement. A wall of solvent drums that only looks tight, with no blocking, is not secured, and skipping the bracing to make the gate does not hold that load on the road.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a square appearance with securement. Friction in a tight wall is not blocking or bracing, so the drums can still shift.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes drum material with securement. Plastic solvent drums still move in a van unless they are blocked and braced.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the floor layer as self-securing. Leaving the bottom free to settle is the opposite of securing the whole stack against movement.

prompt: One carton printed this side up will not stand in the short last row, so a helper tips it onto its side and covers the arrows with the next box. What has to stay visible, and how should that carton sit?

options.text: Hide the arrows so the row looks level for an inspection
Lay it down, because orientation marks matter on the shipper dock and not on the road
Keep labels and arrows visible, and leave it upright
Tip it onto its side whenever the last row is too short to stand it up

explanation: Labels and orientation arrows stay visible, and a this-side-up carton stays upright. A short last row is not a reason to lay that package on its side or to cover the arrows with the next box.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a neat row with a legal load. Covering arrows so the stack looks level hides the marks the rules say must stay visible.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes dock handling with the whole trip. Orientation marks govern how the package rides, not only how it sat at the shipper.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a short row as permission to ignore this side up. The carton stays upright even when the last row is too short to stand another one.

prompt: The overnight forecast is below freezing, and your van holds a flammable load the rules say must stay away from heat. May you run the cargo heater on that trip?

options.text: No. Keep the heater off that material
Yes. A low setting is allowed if you stay with the van and watch it
Yes. The heater ban is a food-load rule, not a rule for this flammable load
Yes. Shut the heater off once you are close to the receiver

explanation: Do not use a cargo heater around a material the rules say must stay away from heat. A freezing forecast does not create an exception for this flammable load, including a low setting or a heater you plan to shut off later.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses supervision with permission. Watching a low heater does not make it legal around a material that must stay away from heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes the heater ban with the food rules. The restriction here is the flammable load and heat, not whether food is also aboard.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a late shutdown as compliance. The heater stays off for the trip, not until you are near the receiver.

prompt: Your codriver lights a cigarette in the bunk while the trailer carries a placarded explosive load and claims the cab does not count. May anyone smoke on this trip?

options.text: Yes. The cab is separate, so smoking there leaves the cargo unaffected
Yes. Smoking is fine once the windows are up and the cargo doors are latched
Yes. The limit applies while you are parked, not after the truck is moving
No. Smoking is not allowed around that placarded load

explanation: Smoking is not allowed around a placarded flammable or explosive load, and the cab is not a smoking lounge for that trip. A cigarette in the bunk still counts while explosives are placarded on the trailer.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the cab with a separate smoking area. The cab is part of the trip, and smoking around a placarded explosive load is not allowed there.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes closed windows and latched doors with permission to smoke. Those steps do not create an exception for a placarded explosive load.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the rule as a parking-lot limit. The ban follows the placarded load on the trip, not only while the truck is standing still.

prompt: A fiber drum of corrosive has a crushed chime and a wet streak, and the clerk says to put it aboard because the receiver is already waiting. What do you do with that damaged drum?

options.text: Wrap the crushed chime and load it so the receiver is not kept waiting
Set it aside and tell the shipper; do not load it
Put it nearest the doors so a later leak is easy to see
Accept it and write the damage on the delivery receipt after you arrive

explanation: A damaged leaking package does not go on the truck. Set the crushed, wet corrosive drum aside and tell the shipper. A waiting receiver does not make that drum fit to load.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a wrap and a schedule with an acceptable package. Covering a crushed, wet chime does not make a damaged drum legal freight.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes an easy look at the doors with acceptance. Placing a leaking drum where you can watch it still means you loaded a package that should have stayed off.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the problem to the delivery receipt. The drum is refused at the dock and the shipper is told now, not after it has ridden to the receiver.

prompt: A carton has a smeared hazard label, and dispatch tells you to cut the tape and look inside so you can choose the trailer placard. How do you identify the contents?

options.text: Open one carton and identify the hazard from whatever sits inside
Guess the class from the weight and the shape of the box
Use the papers and the label; do not open the package
Have a dock worker pour a sample so you can judge the product

explanation: You do not open a package to see what is inside. The shipping papers and the label are the identification, even when the label is smeared and dispatch wants a look before you choose a placard.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an opened carton with identification. Cutting the tape to see the inner containers is not how you determine the hazard or the placard.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes package shape and weight with classification. Guessing a class from the box does not replace the papers and the label.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a poured sample as a field test. Opening and sampling the product is the opposite of leaving the package closed and reading the papers.

prompt: A new driver treats a gasoline cargo tank as a giant non-bulk box and copies the placard plan from yesterday's small-can load without a tank check. What is wrong with that approach?

options.text: Bulk and non-bulk rules differ, so check the tank
A cargo tank is a large box, so yesterday's placard plan applies to it too
Skip placards on a tank because the product name is already painted on the shell
Reuse the small-can plan whenever the hazard class looks familiar

explanation: Bulk and non-bulk follow different rules, so a gasoline cargo tank is not just a big box you placard the same way as yesterday's small cans. Table 1 materials are placarded at any amount and Table 2 materials at 1,001 pounds or more, and you still check the tank instead of copying the non-bulk plan.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a cargo tank with an oversized non-bulk box. Bulk placarding is its own check, not a copy of yesterday's small-can plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes a painted product name with placards. A name on the shell does not replace the placards the tank rules require.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a familiar class as a shortcut. The same class can still follow different placard rules once it is in a cargo tank rather than small cans.

prompt: The hazmat drums already on your trailer put the drive axles near the legal limit, and dispatch says this commodity gets a weight exception for one more pallet. Which weight rule still binds you?

options.text: Add the pallet, because hazmat freight is excused from axle limits
Slide the extra pallet toward the steer axle and ignore the bridge formula
Accept the extra weight if every drum is in a lighter packing group
Stay within the vehicle rating and the bridge formula

explanation: The load must not exceed the weight the vehicle and the bridge formula allow. Hazmat does not get a weight exception you invent, so one more pallet stays off when the drive axles are already near the legal limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a hazmat exception to axle limits. The commodity does not excuse the vehicle rating, even when dispatch says to add a pallet.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes a weight shift with permission to ignore the bridge formula. Moving freight toward the steer axle is not a waiver of that formula.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses packing group with legal weight. A lighter packing group does not raise the weight the vehicle and the bridge formula allow.

prompt: A helper lays acetylene cylinders on their sides across the trailer floor and says horizontal is fine if straps are somewhere in the van. How should those cylinders travel?

options.text: Loose on the floor is acceptable when the valve caps are screwed on tight
Upright and secured, valves protected, unless a rule says otherwise
On their sides is normal whenever the van has no cylinder racks installed
Horizontal and unbraced is acceptable when the gas is not a flammable division

explanation: Cylinders travel upright and secured, with valves protected, unless the rules for that cylinder say otherwise. Straps somewhere in the van do not make acetylene cylinders legal when they are loose on their sides across the floor.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a valve cap with securement. Caps help protect valves, but loose cylinders on the floor are still the miss.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes a missing rack with permission to lay cylinders down. No rack means you still secure them upright unless a rule for that cylinder says otherwise.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a nonflammable division as an exception to upright securement. The miss is loose on the floor, and flammability is not what waives the cylinder rule.

prompt: At a customer rack that is not equipped for transfers, a supervisor asks you to pump flammable liquid from your cargo tank into a tank parked beside you. Should you make that transfer?

options.text: Yes, if both tanks show the same product name on the papers
Yes. Any rack with a hose can move flammable liquid from one tank to another
No. Do not transfer at a rack that is not set up for it
Yes, once you ground the receiving tank and leave your own manhole open

explanation: You do not transfer a flammable liquid from one cargo tank to another at a loading rack you were not told is set up for it. Matching product names and a hose at this customer rack do not make that transfer authorized.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses matching product names with a transfer setup. The same name on both papers does not mean this rack is equipped for tank-to-tank transfer.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes the presence of a hose with an authorized rack. A hose alone does not make a customer rack a place to pump flammable liquid between cargo tanks.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a partial ground and an open manhole as the setup. That is not the equipped transfer the rules require, and an open manhole is a release path.

prompt: You move a hazmat shipment from a closed van onto an open flatbed, and the bills say the packages need weather protection. Does the open deck cancel blocking and cover?

options.text: No. Still block, brace, and cover if the papers require it
Yes. An open flatbed needs straps, so blocking and tarps are optional extras
Yes. Weather protection applies inside a closed van and not on a deck
Yes. An open deck is exempt once the packages already carry labels

explanation: A flatbed still needs the packages blocked, braced, and protected from weather if the papers require it. Moving this shipment from a van to an open deck does not cancel the blocking or the cover the bills call for.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses straps with full flatbed securement. Straps do not replace blocking and bracing, and they do not replace weather protection the papers require.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes the van with the only place weather protection applies. The bills still require that protection on the open deck.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats labels as a substitute for securement and cover. Labels identify the hazard; they do not excuse blocking, bracing, or the weather protection on the papers.

prompt: Two classes the segregation table forbids are already inside one trailer, and the loader says the problem is solved because the milder class sits in the nose. Does that nose position fix the mix?

options.text: Yes. The milder class in front satisfies the segregation table
Yes. Empty pallets between them count as the separation the table requires
Yes. Incompatible classes are acceptable when the front class is the milder one
No. Nose position does not replace segregation

explanation: Incompatible classes in the same trailer with no segregation are not fixed by putting the milder one in front. Nose position is not the segregation table, so that mix stays illegal until the classes are separated as the table requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a front stack with compliance. The milder class in the nose does not satisfy a segregation table that forbids the pair.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes empty pallets with the separation the table specifies. Filler freight between forbidden classes is not a substitute you invent for the table.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a milder hazard as a waiver. Which class is milder does not make a forbidden pair legal in one trailer.

prompt: The drum label says corrosive, the placard handed to you reads flammable, and the shipping paper names an oxidizer for the same freight. What should you do before you accept that shipment?

options.text: Accept the paper and ignore the label and the placard
Use the placard you already have and leave the other marks unchanged
Haul it and let the receiver decide which of the three hazards is real
Refuse it; the label, placard, and paper disagree

explanation: Refuse a shipment when the label, the placard, and the paper name three different hazards. Corrosive, flammable, and oxidizer on the same freight are three different names, so you do not accept it until that conflict is fixed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the shipping paper with the only document that matters. Ignoring a conflicting label and placard leaves three hazard names on one shipment.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes the placard you have on hand with the hazard you are actually offered. Picking a convenient placard does not reconcile the label and the paper.
distractorExplanations.c: Delays the conflict to the receiver. You refuse the mismatched shipment before it is accepted, rather than hauling three different hazard names.

prompt: You are rolling a placarded van on a two-lane road when a steady drip starts under the rear doors and you can still steer. What should you do before anything else?

options.text: Pull off away from people and ignition, then notify responders and your carrier
Keep going to the next truck stop so someone there can find absorbent
Sniff the drip on the shoulder so you can name the product before you call
Stop beside a storefront so the address is easy, and wait in the cab

explanation: You can still steer, so you leave the road away from people and anything that could ignite vapors, then you tell emergency responders and the carrier. Driving the leak to a truck stop spreads the product along the route.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a truck-stop stop with a safe shutdown. Driving a leaking load onward spreads the release; you park clear of people and ignition, then report it.

prompt: A dual tire on your placarded tractor starts throwing smoke on the interstate shoulder after a long grade. Why is that fire a cargo problem, not only a tire problem?

prompt: After a valve fails on a tank of flammable liquid at a rest area, a trooper asks what the papers and the orange guidebook are for. What do those two sources give you?

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a claim file with response information. Insurance details do not tell the trooper the hazard; the papers and guidebook do.

Refuse the pad, because an open fire beside these explosives is forbidden

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses drying damp packs with a safe use of heat. Radiant heat from an open fire is not a drying method for explosive packaging.

prompt: The engine dies on a rural highway with a placarded trailer and you cannot roll it off the traveled lane. What is the right way to protect traffic while you wait?

distractorExplanations.c: Confuses going for help with protecting the scene. Walking away leaves a placarded vehicle unmarked in the lane; you warn traffic and call from the scene.

prompt: A helper at a bulk plant offers you a cigarette while you stand next to an open manway on a Class 3 cargo tank. What is the rule about that cigarette?

prompt: A drum has split inside your box trailer at a crowded truck stop and liquid is spreading on the floor. When you reach emergency help, which facts do you give them first?

The brand printed on the drum and the shipper's billing street

The placard color alone, without opening the papers in the cab

prompt: Your papers show a poison inhalation hazard and a cloud is drifting off the trailer after a gasket lets go. What should the response emphasize while people are moved?

Skip the inhalation guidance and use the general guide page
Walk in from downwind so the cloud is easier to see
Breathing protection and keeping people out of the downwind path

prompt: A pallet marked Division 4.3 is burning on the dock and a coworker reaches for a water hose. Which action is the one that can make this fire worse?

prompt: While you fuel a tractor, diesel splashes your forearm and soaks the cuff of your shirt. Nothing is in your eyes and you are not dizzy. What is the sensible first care for that skin?

Rinse with water alone, because soap drives the fuel into the skin

prompt: A navigation app offers a shorter path through a downtown tunnel for your placarded load, and the state map marks that tunnel off limits. Why do those route limits exist?

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a short path with the purpose of the rule. Routing limits can force a longer designated road because the short path uses a restricted tunnel or a crowded city.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses local streets with the preferred system. These limits usually keep risky loads off tunnels, bridges, and populated routes, not off the freeway and onto neighborhood streets.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses traffic balancing with hazard routing. The limits keep high-risk loads away from tunnels, bridges, and crowded routes; they do not exist to spread trucks evenly.

prompt: At the gate the placard on your trailer says flammable and the papers describe a corrosive with a different identification number. What do you do with the shipment?

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the driver with the shipper who certified the papers. You do not rewrite the papers in the cab to match the placard; the shipper has to fix the discrepancy.

prompt: Before you leave the shipper, you check that emergency response information rides with the papers for this corrosive load. What must that information cover?

distractorExplanations.c: Confuses two classes with the rule. Emergency response information is required for the hazardous materials being transported, including this corrosive, not only explosives and radioactive packages.

prompt: Vapor is leaving a leaking tote in a parking lot and a crowd is gathering on the side the wind is blowing toward. Where should you send those people?

prompt: You find a radioactive package with a torn outer wrap and a crushed corner during a trailer check at a warehouse door. What exposure habit fits this package?

prompt: A cargo tank fitting weeps while the rig remains controllable on a county road next to a schoolyard. Which action follows the leak procedure?

prompt: Smoke pours from a trailer wheel as you approach an exit, and the freight behind that wheel is regulated material. Why is rolling to the next ramp the wrong plan?

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a ramp with a better fire plan. Driving to where water might be easier leaves the burning wheel against the freight; you stop rather than continue.

prompt: You have the guidebook open to the right guide after a release, and a bystander says the book means you can skip the emergency call. What is the guidebook's real job?

prompt: Traffic has stopped inside a tunnel and you could still creep the placarded combination out to the open air. Where must you avoid remaining if you can still move the unit?

A tunnel is acceptable for a consumer commodity, while a bridge is a place you must leave

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses flashers and papers with a legal parking place. Warning lights do not make a tunnel, a bridge, or a spot beside an open flame acceptable when you can still move.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a warning flare with a safe neighbor. An open flame is still an open flame beside a placarded vehicle; you do not remain next to it if you can move.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a consumer-commodity placard with a tunnel exemption. If you can move, you do not remain in the tunnel or on a bridge, and you do not stay beside an open flame.

prompt: Your bill of lading names a required highway, but a side road looks faster around a crash scene. May you take that side road with this load?

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a required route with a suggestion. When the state or the papers restrict the path, you do not drop it because another road looks faster.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses route limits with explosives and poisons alone. A restriction on the papers or from the state still applies; a miscellaneous placard does not make the side road legal.

prompt: A gust lifts your shipping papers out the window at a fuel island and they scatter across a wet lot. What has to happen before this placarded trip continues?

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses placards with shipping papers. Placards do not replace the papers a gust blew out of the cab; you do not continue the trip without them.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a radio reading with papers in the cab. Dispatch reading the entries later still means you left without the papers, which you do not do.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a memory note with the shipping papers. A napkin you write from memory is not the papers; you recover or replace them before the placarded trip continues.

prompt: A small fire starts under the dash of your tractor while a placarded trailer is coupled and people are standing nearby. What do you do about the trailer doors?

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a look inside with the right move. Opening the trailer to check the freight is the miss; you get people away, call for help, and leave the doors shut.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the next ramp with a safer inspection point. Driving a dash fire to another ramp keeps the fire with the placarded trailer; you get people away and call for help.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses airing the freight with control. Uncoupling and opening the doors before you call is the opposite of leaving the trailer shut and getting help.

prompt: You want a hot meal and the placarded tractor is idling in front of a diner, out of your sight once you sit down. What attendance rule are you about to break?

A meal is fine if you leave the papers on the driver's seat and lock the door
Attendance applies to explosives, not to a placarded flammable liquid at a diner

distractorExplanations.c: Confuses papers on the seat with a driver on the scene. The papers do not attend the vehicle; you do, and an unseen idling tractor at the diner breaks that rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses explosives with the attendance rule. A placarded flammable liquid still has to be attended; the diner stop does not drop that duty.

prompt: You pull a placarded cargo tank up to a diesel island where another driver is smoking beside a glowing space heater. How do you fuel this unit?

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses live gauges with a legal fueling setup. The engine stays off, smoking is not allowed, and you do not fuel beside the heater.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses wind direction with the smoking rule. Upwind or not, smoking beside the fueling is forbidden, and the engine is off.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a space heater with something the rules ignore. A glowing heater is an ignition source; you do not fuel the placarded tank beside it.

prompt: Responders are on scene after a leak from your placarded trailer and they ask for the shipping papers. A coworker says to hide them so the company avoids trouble. What do you do?

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses shielding the company with the driver's duty. Hiding the papers because a fine feels likely is the miss; responders get the papers so they know what leaked.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the placard legend with the papers. A placard is not the shipping papers, and claiming none were issued keeps the identity from the responders who need it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a later phone call with the scene. Responders need the papers now; finishing the deliveries and pointing them to the shipper next week withholds the information.

prompt: A poison package has broken open on the shoulder of a ramp and powder is on the pavement around your boots. What is the right work for you at that spot?
