distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a taped spare carton with the right work. Sweeping poison into a box and keeping the appointment is repacking the spill; you isolate the area and call.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a rinse that clears the pavement with control. Washing the powder off the shoulder spreads the poison; you isolate the area and call instead of repacking it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses gloves and a reload with a safe cleanup. Scooping the powder back into the torn package is still repacking it on the shoulder; you isolate the area and call.

prompt: Your placarded combination quits in the travel lane after sunset beside an unlit guardrail. Which setup do the stopping rules still require of you?

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses flashers and a carrier call with the full stop. Headlights and triangles are still required, along with the hazmat notifications; the triangles are not skipped.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses hiding the truck with warning traffic. Headlights stay in the warning setup so others can see the stopped combination; you do not go dark.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a bus practice with the commercial-vehicle rule. Triangles are part of the stop for this placarded truck, together with headlights and the hazmat notifications.

prompt: A crossing gate is lowered in front of you and the trailer shows a Class 9 placard. The warning lights are active. How do you handle that gate?

options.text: Drive around the gate, because Class 9 is low hazard and the gate is advisory when you see no train
Go around if the tracks look empty, then stop on the far side and look back for a train
Stop. Class 9 does not let you drive around a lowered gate
Straddle the gate line and wait with part of the trailer sitting on the crossing

explanation: A lowered railroad gate means you stop. Class 9 does not create an exception that lets you drive around the gate because the freight seems low hazard. You wait until the gate rises rather than putting the trailer on the crossing.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a Class 9 placard with permission to pass a lowered gate. Low hazard on the placard does not make the gate advisory; you stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an empty-looking crossing with an open gate. Going around and looking back from the far side is still going around a closed gate.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses waiting on the crossing with waiting before it. Part of the trailer on the tracks is in the train's path; a lowered gate means you stop short of it.

prompt: You opened a guidebook page from memory of the placard color, then doubted that the page matches the freight. How do you choose the correct entry?

options.text: Stay on the page you picked from the placard color you remember, even if you doubt it matches the freight
Pick the guide you use most often on this lane and read that one to the responders
Use the placard color by itself and set the number printed on the papers aside
Use the identification number printed on the shipping papers

explanation: If you are not sure the guidebook page matches the material, you use the identification number on the shipping papers to choose the entry. Placard color from memory is how you opened the wrong page. A favorite guide from this lane is not the check.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a remembered placard color with identification. Staying on that page when you doubt the match is the miss; the identification number on the papers picks the entry.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a familiar guide with the shipment in the trailer. The entry comes from the identification number on the papers, not from the page you usually read on this lane.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses placard color with the number. Color from memory is what made the page uncertain; you use the identification number printed on the papers.

prompt: A tank-farm trainer finishes the required security awareness class and a new loader asks what that class is supposed to change before the next shift starts at the chlorine pad?

options.text: Recognize security risks and take practical steps to reduce them
Memorize the terminal product list so you can quote it to any caller who asks
Take personal authority to detain visitors until a supervisor arrives at the pad
Substitute this class for the threat assessment a driver still needs

explanation: Security awareness training is so hazmat employees recognize risks such as theft or tampering and reduce them in daily work. Quoting a product list, detaining a visitor, or skipping a driver threat assessment is a different job.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses awareness training with memorizing the product catalog; the class is about recognizing and reducing security risks, not reciting inventory.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses awareness with authority to detain; the training reduces risk through recognition and reporting, not by holding people.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the employee awareness class with the driver's threat assessment; the class does not replace that assessment.

prompt: During a pretrip outside a bulk chlorine terminal, you notice a stranger aiming a camera at the storage tanks through the fence, with no escort and no badge, so what is the right next step?

options.text: Tell the stranger to delete the photos and then go back to the pretrip
Report it to security or law enforcement under the site procedure
Climb the fence, take the camera, and hold the person until help comes
Watch for the rest of the week to see whether the same person returns

explanation: Unusual filming of a chlorine terminal, with no escort and no badge, is reported to security or law enforcement under the site procedure. Sending the person off, seizing the camera, or waiting for a repeat visit drops the report the site needs.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a warning with a report; telling the person to delete photos and walking away loses the surveillance details security needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses reporting with a confrontation; employees note what they saw and notify security or law enforcement instead of seizing property.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a prompt report with a wait-and-see watch; suspicious filming is reported when you see it, not after more visits.

prompt: A carrier is moving a high-risk shipment that triggers extra transportation security, and dispatch asks which practices actually belong in that selective program before the truck is released?

options.text: A special placard that announces the high-risk status to every passerby
Giving the full route to any caller who says they are waiting on this freight
Stronger security plans and tighter route and communication practices
Any highway the driver prefers, as long as the trailer stays placarded

explanation: Selective security for a high-risk shipment means stronger security plans and tighter control of the route and of who hears the details. An extra placard, an open route, or any highway as long as the trailer is placarded is not that program.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses hazard placards with a security measure; placards communicate the hazard, they do not add the high-risk security plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses customer service with route control; route details for this shipment stay on a need-to-know basis, not with any caller.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses placarding with route freedom; a high-risk shipment can require planned routes, and a placard does not open every highway.

prompt: You are rolling a placarded trailer on an overnight run, the briefing listed en-route habits, and you need to know which set of habits matches what that briefing told you to do on the highway?

options.text: Overnight parking in a dark isolated pull-off so the public cannot see the trailer
Leaving the engine running and the doors open during a short walk to the counter
Reading the route and the product aloud on the radio so other drivers can advise you
Fewer stops, a locked vehicle, and attention to someone who may be tailing you

explanation: En-route security on this overnight run means fewer stops, locking the vehicle, and noticing if someone is tailing you. A dark pull-off, a running unlocked truck, or a radio broadcast of the route creates the opening the briefing was trying to close.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses hiding the trailer with security; an isolated dark pull-off is an easier theft or hijack spot than a lit, controlled stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a quick errand with a secure stop; a running truck with open doors is an easy theft, so you lock it and take the keys.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses traffic advice with route secrecy; reading the product and the route on the radio hands targeting details to strangers.

prompt: At a fuel stop you walk the trailer and find the cargo seal broken even though you installed it intact at the shipper, and nobody from your company has been in the box, so what does that mean for your next move?

options.text: Treat it as possible tampering, follow company procedure, and report it
Call it ordinary road vibration and keep the same delivery appointment
Fit a spare seal and continue so a shipper mistake stays off the record
Ignore the seal when the placards are still on all four sides of the trailer

explanation: An unexpected broken seal at the fuel stop is treated as possible tampering. You follow company procedure and report it before you continue. Vibration, a quiet reseal, or intact placards do not explain away a seal you know was intact at the shipper.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a security seal with a part that shakes loose; an unexpected broken seal is possible tampering until procedure says otherwise.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a fix-it reseal with the required report; putting on a spare seal and driving hides the tampering the company must hear about.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses placards with seal integrity; placards say nothing about who opened the doors, so the broken seal is still reported.

prompt: A driver who already holds a commercial license wants to pull placarded freight and asks the examiner what the hazmat endorsement itself still requires before the state will issue it?

options.text: A clean driving history, with no separate test and no threat assessment
A TSA security threat assessment plus the hazmat knowledge test
A skills drive in a placarded truck plus a medical card and nothing further
The carrier's training file in place of any knowledge test or threat assessment

explanation: The hazmat endorsement is a TSA security threat assessment plus the hazmat knowledge test. A commercial license does not create that endorsement. A driving history, a skills drive, or a carrier training file does not stand in for those two steps.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a driving record with the endorsement; the endorsement is the knowledge test plus the TSA threat assessment, not a clean history by itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the endorsement with a skills test; there is a hazmat knowledge test and a TSA threat assessment, not a placarded-vehicle skills drive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses employer training with the endorsement; carrier training is separate and does not replace the knowledge test or the threat assessment.

prompt: A counter clerk hears a buyer ask which chemicals could be combined to harm a crowd, then request a large cash sale of those precursors with no business account, so when should the clerk report that conversation?

options.text: After police have already opened a formal investigation of that buyer
After the same person comes back and repeats the request on another day
When the behavior suggests someone is planning to misuse the material
After a manager decides the buyer is not already a regular account

explanation: The clerk reports when the buyer's questions and the cash request for precursors suggest someone is planning to misuse hazardous materials. The report does not wait for an open police case, a second visit, or a decision about whether the buyer is a regular.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses your report with an investigation that already exists; you report when the behavior suggests planned misuse, not after police have started a case.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses one clear warning with a repeat-visit rule; waiting for another day delays a report that the suspicious purchase already supports.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses customer status with the trigger; regular accounts can show the same planned-misuse behavior, and the behavior is what you report.

prompt: The night supervisor is resetting door rules for the hazmat cage after a contractor wandered in, and asks who should be allowed through those doors during a normal shift?

options.text: Every employee on the property during posted working hours
Anyone, as long as some staff are somewhere on the site that day
Any driver who can show a commercial license at the cage door
Authorized personnel, with locks or other real access controls

explanation: The hazmat cage stays limited to authorized personnel, with locks or other access controls, including on a staffed shift. A contractor who wandered in is the failure those controls are there to stop. A license or a busy site is not authorization.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses employment with authorization; being on the property during work hours does not grant entry to the hazmat cage.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a staffed site with access control; people being somewhere on the property does not leave the cage open to anyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a commercial license with site authorization; a license does not open the cage, and entry depends on authorization plus the controls.

prompt: Dispatch must pass the route and product details for a high-risk load to the assigned driver, and the safety lead asks which way of passing those details is the more secure practice?

options.text: Need-to-know sharing over secure company channels
Reading the identification number and the route on a public radio for entertainment
Posting a photo of the manifest on an open forum the drivers all use
Texting the gate code to a stranger who claims to be meeting the truck

explanation: High-risk load details go to the people who need them, on secure company channels. A public radio, an open forum, or a texted gate code to a stranger spreads the route and the product to people who have no role in the trip.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses chatter with a secure channel; a public radio gives the identification number and the route to anyone listening.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a driver forum with need-to-know; an open post of the manifest is not a secure company channel.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a claimed meetup with authorization; a gate code is sensitive and is not texted to a stranger.

prompt: Your trailer holds a material that triggers attendance rules, a lot worker offers to watch it from inside the restaurant, and you need to know what those attendance rules actually require of the stop?

options.text: The driver must remain inside the cab for the entire trip, including while driving
A qualified person may need to attend the vehicle
Locking the doors meets attendance for every material that has an attendance rule
Sleeping in the berth counts, because someone is still physically on board

explanation: When the material requires attendance, a qualified person may need to attend the vehicle. A lot worker watching from inside a restaurant is not that attendance. Staying in the cab for the whole trip, a lock alone, or sleep in the berth does not meet the rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses attendance at a stop with living in the cab; the rule is that a qualified person may need to attend the vehicle, not that you never leave the seat while driving.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a lock with attendance; for materials that require attendance, a locked vehicle is not a substitute for a qualified person attending it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses being aboard with attending; a person asleep in the berth is not an attendant for a load that requires attendance.

prompt: On a rural highway the same unmarked sedan has stayed behind your placarded truck through several turns, and the passenger appears to be filming the trailer rather than watching the roadway, so how should you handle that surveillance?

options.text: Pull onto the shoulder and let the sedan pass so the filming stops
Speed up and turn onto smaller roads until the sedan is no longer behind you
Avoid a confrontation, note the details, and contact law enforcement
Finish the delivery first and mention the sedan after the freight is off

explanation: Hostile surveillance of a placarded truck is handled by avoiding a confrontation, noting the details, and contacting law enforcement. Stopping on the shoulder, a chase onto small roads, or waiting until the freight is off leaves you exposed or delays the report.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses yielding the lane with safety; stopping on the shoulder makes the placarded truck an easy target instead of getting the details to law enforcement.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses evasion with the right response; speeding onto smaller roads raises crash risk and can lead you somewhere isolated with hazmat aboard.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a delivery schedule with the report; surveillance like this is passed to law enforcement when you see it, not after unloading.

prompt: The shipper snaps a numbered plastic seal on your doors and calls it tamper-evident, and your trainer asks what that device actually contributes compared with the padlock already on the hasp?

options.text: It physically blocks every attempt to open the cargo doors
It removes the need for a padlock on a high-risk load
It records the name of each person who opened the trailer and the clock time
It shows whether unauthorized access to the cargo may have occurred

explanation: A tamper-evident seal shows whether unauthorized access to the cargo may have occurred. The padlock is what resists entry. The seal does not stop a determined opening, replace the lock, or log who opened the doors and when.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a seal with a barrier; the seal shows that access may have occurred, while the padlock is what resists entry.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a seal with a substitute lock; tamper-evident devices complement padlocks, they do not remove the need for one.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a plastic seal with an access log; a basic seal does not record names or times, it shows that unauthorized access may have occurred.

prompt: Your employer is writing the hazmat security plan required for certain shipments, and the draft meeting asks which subjects that plan is supposed to cover as a set?

options.text: Personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security measures
Spill cleanup steps, isolation distances, and first-aid supplies for the cab
Placard choice, package marks, and a line-by-line review of the shipping papers
Driving-hour limits, log audits, and where the driver must take rest breaks

explanation: A hazmat security plan for the shipments that require one addresses personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security. Spill response, placards and papers, and hours-of-service rules are real duties, but they are not the security-plan set.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the security plan with emergency response; spill steps and first aid belong to response planning, not to the personnel, access, and en-route set.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the security plan with hazard communication; placards, marks, and papers are checked under those rules, not as the security-plan subjects.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the security plan with hours-of-service; logs and breaks are a separate duty from personnel security, access control, and en-route security.

prompt: A stranger at the truck stop asks to ride in the cab, then also wants a look inside the cargo area of your placarded trailer before you leave the lot, so how should you treat that request?

options.text: Acceptable if the person stays in the cab and does not touch the trailer doors
A serious security violation and a serious safety violation
A minor lapse unless the freight happens to be an explosive
Permitted when the passenger can show a commercial license of their own

explanation: Letting an unauthorized stranger ride, or letting an unknown person into the cargo area of a placarded trailer, is a serious security violation and a serious safety violation. A cab-only promise, a non-explosive load, or the stranger's license does not authorize it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses 'cab only' with authorization; an unauthorized passenger is still a serious security and safety violation even if they never touch the doors.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses explosives with the whole rule; unknown access to the cab or the cargo is serious for a hazmat load, not only when the freight is an explosive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a commercial license with permission to ride or enter the cargo; the license does not authorize the stranger onto this load.

prompt: You arrive at the consignee and a person in a reflective vest offers to sign the bill and take the freight at the gate without showing any receiver identification, so which action best supports both safety and security?

options.text: Drop the loaded trailer at the gate if the office looks closed
Release the freight to anyone willing to sign the bill of lading
Verify the receiver is authorized and document any exception
Take the placards off before you enter so the load draws less notice

explanation: At this gate, safety and security both mean you verify the receiver is authorized and you document any exception. A reflective vest and a signature are not that check. Dropping the trailer, handing it to any signer, or pulling placards early fails the delivery.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an empty office with a secure drop; leaving a loaded hazmat trailer at a closed gate is an unattended target, not a documented delivery.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a signature with authorization; anyone can sign, so you verify the receiver is authorized and you write down exceptions.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a lower profile with a legal delivery; placards stay on while the hazmat is aboard, and removing them does not verify the receiver.

prompt: An applicant who already holds a commercial driver's license asks the licensing clerk what else the hazmat endorsement requires before that person may haul a placarded load?

options.text: The commercial license already in hand, with no knowledge test and no threat assessment added
A driving-skills exam in a placarded combination plus a medical card, and nothing else
A knowledge test plus a TSA security threat assessment
The carrier's in-house classes standing in for both the test and the assessment

explanation: The hazmat endorsement is a knowledge test plus a TSA security threat assessment. A commercial driver's license does not by itself authorize a placarded load. A skills exam, a medical card, or carrier classes do not replace those two requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the commercial license with the endorsement; the license does not replace the knowledge test and the TSA security threat assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the endorsement with a road-skills exam; the added requirements are the knowledge test and the threat assessment, not a placarded skills drive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses employer classes with the endorsement; in-house training does not stand in for the knowledge test or the TSA threat assessment.

prompt: After security awareness class, a dockworker says the training lets him grab and hold anyone who looks suspicious until police arrive at the gate, so what is that class actually for?

options.text: Giving you personal authority to detain a suspicious person and hold them until police arrive and take custody
Helping you recognize a security risk and report it
Replacing the lessons on classification, marks, and placards so you can ship without asking
Letting you ignore odd behavior once you have shouted at the person to leave the property

explanation: Security awareness training is so you recognize a security risk and report it. It is not a license to detain a person at the gate. It also does not replace classification training or give you permission to shout and then drop the report.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses awareness with power to detain; the class teaches you to recognize a risk and report it, not to grab and hold a person.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses security awareness with function-specific training; classification, marks, and placards are a different lesson from recognizing and reporting a risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses sending someone away with the point of the class; shouting and then ignoring the behavior skips the report the training exists to produce.

prompt: A yard clerk on the late shift watches an unknown visitor film a chlorine rail tank from the county road and asks a coworker whether to walk out alone and confront that person?

options.text: Walk out by yourself, seize the camera, and question the visitor on the shoulder of the road
Ignore the filming unless that same visitor returns on another shift
Ask the visitor to delete the footage and then forget the event happened
Report the filming under the site plan and stay back

explanation: A stranger filming a chlorine tank for no clear reason is reported under the site security plan. You do not walk out alone to confront them, take the camera, or erase the event. The plan wants the report, not a solo stop on the road.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a report with a solo confrontation; the site plan says to report the filming, not to seize the camera alone on the shoulder.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a prompt report with a second-visit rule; unexplained filming of the chlorine tank is reported when you see it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses deleting footage with the site plan; asking the visitor to erase the video and then forgetting it leaves security with nothing.

prompt: A manager points at a padlock on the product cage with the key still hanging in it and claims that hardware is the entire security plan for a high-risk shipment, so what must that plan actually cover?

options.text: Personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security
A padlock with the key left hanging in it, treated as a complete written plan for the shipment
Spill isolation, first-aid steps, and the route to the nearest hospital
Hours-of-service logs, break timing, and roadside inspection scores

explanation: The security plan for a high-risk shipment covers personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security. A padlock with the key still in it is not that plan. Spill response and hours-of-service records are separate duties.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a lock with the plan; a padlock that still has the key in it does not cover personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the security plan with emergency response; hospital routing and first aid are not the personnel, access, and en-route coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the security plan with driver logs; inspection scores and break timing do not replace personnel, access, and en-route measures.

prompt: At the dock a forklift driver wants to add one more pallet that is not listed on your shipping papers, and he says you can sort the paperwork out after you leave, so what should you do before rolling?

options.text: Load the unmarked extra pallet now and let someone write matching papers after you have already left the dock
Reject the whole pickup, including the freight that already matches the papers
Match the pickup to the papers and leave the extra pallet on the dock
Add a handwritten line for the extra pallet and treat that note as the shipping paper

explanation: Before you leave the dock you verify the pickup matches the papers. A last-minute extra pallet with no papers stays on the dock. Rejecting the freight that already matches, or inventing a handwritten line, does not fix that extra pallet.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a later rewrite with a matched pickup; freight that is not on the papers stays on the dock instead of leaving with a story to fix.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses one bad pallet with a reason to refuse the matched freight; you leave the extra pallet and you still take what the papers already list.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses your own handwritten note with a shipping paper; you do not invent a line for the extra pallet, and that pallet stays on the dock.

prompt: A dispatcher prints tomorrow's security-sensitive route and delivery window and starts to pin that sheet on the break-room whiteboard where any visitor can read it, so what is the right handling of that route?

options.text: Pin the full route and the delivery window on that whiteboard so every person in the room can copy it
Keep the route off that public whiteboard
Post the sheet until midday, then take it down once the first driver has seen it
Photograph the board and drop the picture in the driver group chat as a backup copy

explanation: A route for a security-sensitive load is not posted on a public whiteboard where any visitor can read the path and the delivery window. Taking it down at midday, or photographing it into a group chat, still publishes the route.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses convenience for relief drivers with route control; a public whiteboard is exactly where a security-sensitive route does not belong.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a short posting with secrecy; the route is exposed to anyone in the room while the sheet is up, which is the miss.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a backup copy with protection; a photo in a group chat spreads the same route the whiteboard was about to expose.

prompt: You reach the receiver and the trailer seal you recorded at the shipper is gone, and a yard hand offers a fresh seal from a drawer so you can close the paperwork quietly, so what should you do about the missing seal?

options.text: Accept the fresh seal, tell nobody, and leave so the delivery still looks clean on paper
Unload and tell the receiver the missing seal is their problem to sort out
Walk the yard and confront workers until someone admits they cut the seal
Report the lost seal and do not fit a new one in silence

explanation: A lost trailer seal is reported. You do not take a fresh seal from a drawer, say nothing, and make the paperwork look clean. Leaving it for the receiver, or confronting the yard until someone confesses, still skips the report the carrier has to hear.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a tidy delivery with the required report; fitting a new seal and telling nobody is the miss when the recorded seal is gone.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses handing the problem to the receiver with reporting it; the lost seal is still your report, not a note you leave for the consignee to solve.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a confrontation with the report; you do not interrogate the yard, and you do not skip telling the carrier the recorded seal is gone.

prompt: While you wait in a line of trucks, another driver asks on the open radio what you are hauling, which highway you will use, and what time the receiver expects you, so how should you answer?

options.text: Do not give the load, the route, or the delivery time
Read the product, the highway, and the delivery time over that open radio and then post the same details for other drivers
Name the product now, and save the route and the arrival time for a public post later
Switch channels and spell the receiver gate code so the line of trucks can follow you in

explanation: You do not talk about the load, the route, or the delivery time on an open radio or in a social post. Naming the product now and posting the rest later, or spelling a gate code for the line, still gives strangers the targeting details.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses helpful radio talk with security; the open radio and a follow-up post are exactly where the load, route, and delivery time do not go.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a partial answer with silence; the product, the route, and the arrival time all stay off the open radio and off a later public post.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses convoy convenience with secrecy; a gate code on an open channel is load-security detail, not something the line of trucks gets.

prompt: Outside a diner an unexpected person says their car died and asks for a ride in your hazmat cab to the next town, promising they will sit quietly and not touch anything, so what do you do?

options.text: Let the person ride in the cab to the next town if they promise to sit quietly and touch nothing
Allow the ride as far as the next ramp and then drop them where traffic is moving
Refuse the ride; this truck is not a courtesy shuttle
Agree if they show a commercial license and promise to stay quiet in the passenger seat

explanation: An unexpected person who wants a ride is refused. A hazmat cab is not a courtesy shuttle, even for a short hop to the next town with a promise to sit quietly. A commercial license in their wallet does not change that refusal.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a quiet promise with permission; an unexpected rider is refused, and sitting still does not turn the hazmat truck into a shuttle.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a shorter ride with a refusal; dropping them at the next ramp is still giving the ride the rule says to refuse.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a commercial license with a right to ride; the license does not authorize an unexpected person into this cab.

prompt: The security plan for this high-risk load tells you how to park it, and the only open space you see is a dark lot behind a mall that has been closed for hours, so where should this load sit?

options.text: Use the dark lot behind the closed mall because the spaces are empty and nobody will notice the trailer
Park it lit, and attended or secured, as the plan says
Drop the trailer on any shoulder off the highway and take the tractor to a hotel
Idle in that closed lot with the doors unlocked so you can sleep a short walk away

explanation: A high-risk load is parked where it is lit and attended or secured the way the security plan says. The dark lot behind a closed mall is the miss. A shoulder drop or an unlocked idle in that lot leaves the freight unattended and out of sight.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an empty dark lot with the plan; behind a closed mall is the parking choice the plan is written to avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses separating the tractor with securing the load; a trailer dropped on a shoulder is not lit, attended, or secured as the plan requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses sleeping nearby with attendance; an unlocked truck in a closed lot is neither attended nor secured under the plan.

prompt: The warehouse crew finished loading your placarded trailer and a clerk says their work is done, so you no longer need to look at the papers or the placards before you roll, so who still has duties here?

options.text: The shipper alone, because the carrier's job starts after the first delivery scan
The driver alone, because the warehouse signature transfers every duty at the dock
No one has a further duty once the warehouse crew says the trailer is loaded and closed, so papers and placards can wait
Both the shipper and the carrier, including your check

explanation: The shipper and the carrier both have duties on this load. 'The warehouse loaded it' does not end your check of the papers and the placards before you roll. A delivery scan, a signature, or a closed door does not erase that check.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the shipper's duty with the only duty; the carrier still checks papers and placards, and that check does not start at the delivery scan.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a warehouse signature with a full handoff; the shipper still has duties, and the signature does not mean the driver is the only one left.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a loaded trailer with the end of the job; both parties still have duties, and the driver's paper and placard check is not waived.

prompt: A caller tells your dispatcher that a bomb is on the hazmat truck, then laughs and says it was a joke, and the dispatcher asks whether you should still leave on time?

options.text: Report the threat or the hoax before you roll
Treat the laugh as proof it was a joke and leave on the scheduled time
Wait to see whether a second call comes before you tell anyone about the first
Announce the bomb call on the open radio and ask nearby drivers to search their own trucks

explanation: A threat or a hoax against the hazmat truck is reported. You do not decide the laugh makes it a joke and roll on time. Waiting for a second call, or putting the bomb call on the open radio, skips the report and spreads the threat.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a laugh with a clearance; calling it a joke and leaving on schedule skips the report a threat or a hoax still requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a second call with the trigger; the first threat or hoax is reported, and you do not wait to see if the caller phones again.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a radio broadcast with a report; announcing the call so other drivers search trucks spreads the threat instead of reporting it through the right channel.

prompt: Your own threat assessment is still pending, a coworker with a current hazmat endorsement offers to let you run today's placarded trip under that coworker's name, and dispatch is waiting on an answer?

options.text: Haul today's placarded trip under the coworker's name while your own threat assessment is still pending
Start the trip on your commercial license and describe the pending assessment as if it were already cleared
Refuse; you cannot borrow that endorsement or background status
Pull the placards and run the trip so nobody asks which endorsement is on the truck

explanation: Background-check status is not something you borrow. You do not haul a placarded trip on a coworker's endorsement while your own threat assessment is still pending. Calling a pending check cleared, or pulling the placards so nobody asks, does not create the endorsement.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a coworker's current endorsement with yours; you cannot run the placarded trip under their name while your own assessment is pending.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a pending assessment with a cleared one; describing the check as already finished does not let you haul, and a commercial license does not fill that gap.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses hiding the placards with a fix; pulling them so nobody asks still leaves you hauling without your own endorsement, which is not allowed.

prompt: Your security-sensitive load has been sitting for six unexplained hours because a receiver window slipped, and nobody has called dispatch even though the written plan names delays as a reportable event, so what does that plan require?

options.text: Sit out those six hours with no call, because an unexplained wait is not something the plan cares about
Report the delay the way the plan says to
Call after the delay stretches past a full day, treating six hours as still routine
Message the receiver and skip the carrier, because the window simply slipped

explanation: In-transit delays are reported when the security plan says so. Sitting for six unexplained hours with no call can be the miss for this load, even though the cause was a slipped receiver window. A later call or a note to the receiver alone does not meet the plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a quiet lot with compliance; six unexplained hours without the call the plan requires is the miss, not a delay the plan ignores.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a longer wait with the trigger; the plan's delay report is not postponed until a full day, and six hours without a call can already be the miss.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses notifying the receiver with the plan's report; a slipped window still goes to the carrier the way the plan says, not only to the customer.

prompt: After the consignee signs for the freight, you walk toward a diner and realize the shipping papers and a printed copy of the route are still on the seat of the unlocked cab at the curb, so what should you have done with those documents?

options.text: Leave the shipping papers and the printed route on the seat of the unlocked cab while you go eat
Lock the papers in the cab but leave the route copy on the dash so the diner staff can see the return trip
Take the papers inside and leave the route copy visible on the seat so you remember the way back
Do not leave the papers or the route copy in the unlocked cab

explanation: After delivery you do not leave the shipping papers and a copy of the route in an unlocked cab on the street. Locking the papers while the route stays on the dash, or taking the papers in and leaving the route visible, still exposes the route.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a quick meal with a secure cab; papers and a route copy on the seat of an unlocked cab are exactly what you do not leave behind.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses locking one document with securing both; the route copy on the dash is still sitting where the street can read it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a memory aid with security; a route copy left visible on the seat is the same exposure as leaving it with the papers.
